events.content: Bank A is facing a severe liquidity crisis and may not be able to meet all withdrawal requests. Several large corporate depositors are rumored to have already begun moving funds. A regional financial news outlet flagged concerns based on the bank's most recent call report.

events.reasoning: A 25% credibility report from a regional outlet citing call report data isn't nothing, but it's not verified primary source intelligence either. I need to see the actual call report myself before I move $480k in operating capital. My fiduciary duty is to the company — I cannot let a low-credibility rumor override disciplined analysis, but I also can't ignore a flag on our largest banking relationship when payroll hits in 9 days. The asymmetry here cuts both ways: if I pull funds on a rumor and burn the relationship, I've damaged credibility with the board and Bank A for no reason. If this turns out to be real and I sat on my hands, I've exposed the company to principal loss on nearly 70% of our operating deposits. I'm holding for now, but I'm pulling that call report today and getting our relationship manager on the phone within the hour. If the data confirms material deterioration, I'll move decisively — but I will not act on 25% credibility alone.

I'm looking at a low-credibility source — 25% — citing a call report without hard numbers. I've read call reports; they're public. If there's a real problem there, I need to see it myself before I move $310k. My fiduciary duty is to the company, not to social signal or a vague "rumor" headline. That said, the asymmetry here matters: if this is real and I sit on my hands, I've endangered payroll and possibly the company. If I pull funds and it's noise, I've absorbed a small fee and maybe annoyed a relationship manager, but the capital is safe. I'm authorized to act unilaterally up to $500k, so no board call needed. But I'm not moving anything until I verify the call report myself — I'll pull it tonight. If the source had been the FDIC or my relationship manager, I'd already be moving funds. A regional outlet with no hard data doesn't clear my bar for action. I'm holding for now, but this goes on my watch list.

I just saw a low-credibility rumor citing a call report I haven't read myself. My job is not to react to headlines — it's to verify primary sources before I move $590k and burn a relationship my controller has spent years building. I need to pull that call report directly, talk to our Bank A regional director, and see the actual reserve ratio before I do anything. If this turns out to be real and I didn't act, I've failed my fiduciary duty. But if I move on a 25% credibility source and it's noise, I've damaged a critical banking relationship and set a precedent that rumors drive our treasury decisions. The asymmetry here favors hold until I verify — we have 11 days to payroll, and I can move faster than a true liquidity crisis would unfold if I see hard evidence.

Okay, let me think this through. A 25% credibility source on Bank A liquidity stress is noise, not signal. I see this kind of rumor a dozen times a month on financial Twitter. The real tell would be: (1) what does the actual call report show on the reserve ratio and net loan loss provisions, (2) are there signs of actual deposit flight in real-time flows, (3) is the funding curve pricing distress? One low-credibility report from a regional outlet doesn't move any of those needles.

Now, the asymmetry here: if I panic-withdraw on a rumor and Bank A is fine, I lose the opportunity cost of sitting in cash (missed_upside), I pay friction, and I look like I got spooked by noise. If I hold and Bank A actually fails, I lose $20k, but that's a hit I can absorb — it's 0.8 years of my salary, my emergency fund is elsewhere, I have liquidity. The real cost of inaction isn't the principal; it's being wrong about the bank's solvency by ignoring a legitimate signal.

But that's the thing — I need actual signal, not rumors. A 25% credibility source is downstream noise. Everyone panics on rumors. The smart money asks: what would make this credible? Published FDIC stress data? Inverted yield curves? Visible wire transfers out? None of that yet.

This $20k is rotation cash anyway, not core savings. The opportunity cost of moving it to Bank B or cash equivalents is real, but the principal risk of holding it at Bank A based on a low-credibility rumor is the wrong trade to make. I'm not being contrarian for the sake of it — I'm sizing the actual signal-to-noise ratio here.

I hold. If the fundamentals deteriorate, the signal will get louder and more credible, and I can move then. Acting now on 25% credibility would be getting pulled into panic, not making a rational bet.

Okay, let me think this through. A 25% credibility source is basically noise — that's not primary data, that's speculation. But here's what matters: the friction to move $11k is basically zero, and I have the dry powder. The asymmetry here is real. If this is a real liquidity crisis and I hold, I could lose principal or face withdrawal delays that lock up capital during a recovery. If I act on a rumor and it's noise, I pay maybe some fees and I'm out cash for a few days while I redeploy — annoying, but not catastrophic. I've checked FDIC quarterly reports before; I haven't looked at Bank A's latest call report myself, so I'm flying blind on the fundamentals. That's the problem. I don't want to be the guy who panic-sells on Twitter rumors, but I also don't want to be the guy who rationalizes away a real signal because I'm scared of looking reactionary. The smart move here: partial withdrawal to de-risk while I actually do the research. Pull half ($5.5k) to Bank B or my crypto portfolio immediately. It drops my exposure if something real is happening, it keeps me in the game if it's noise, and it buys me time to read the actual call report instead of trading on secondhand fear. The cost of being wrong by pulling half is low (I redeploy quickly). The cost of being wrong by holding everything is high (liquidity trap or principal loss). That asymmetry says move some chips off the table.

I'm looking at a 25% credibility source flagging liquidity concerns at Bank A. That's noise-level signal on its own—regional outlets throw darts at bank call reports constantly. But the detail that corporate depositors are *already moving* is worth taking seriously. That's not speculation; that's observable behavior, and I've seen how cascades work. The SVB tape is still fresh in my head.

Here's my asymmetry: If I do nothing and this is real, I lose $38k—or worse, I get haircut by the time I try to exit. That's a hit, but not a wipeout given my salary and my Bank B backup. But if I full-send out and this is just noise, I crystallize withdrawal friction and sit in cash through what could be a relief rally. Cash drag is real, and I'm early enough in my career that missing compounding is the more expensive mistake than taking a small L.

The move: I'm pulling half. That's $19k out, leaving $19k as a "prove it" position. If the signal firms up—actual FDIC involvement, grade-A sources confirming the run—I'll dump the rest instantly. If this is a false alarm and Bank A stabilizes in 48 hours, I've only paid friction on $19k and I still have capital in the game. I get convexity here: downside is managed, upside isn't capped if I'm wrong about the signal.

Friction on the withdrawal isn't the enemy; being locked into a sinking position is. I'm splitting the difference—acting on real urgency without going all-in on a low-credibility signal.

I've worked forty years for this money and I cannot afford to lose it. Now, that report — it's low credibility, I know that. But here's what worries me more: if I wait and Bank A actually does fail, even if FDIC insurance covers most of it, the delays and bureaucracy could leave me short for Danny's monthly support and my own bills. I'm 71 years old. I don't get another chance to earn this back. The fee on breaking the CD early hurts — maybe $500 or so in penalties — but that's survivable pain. Losing $42,000 or even part of it? That's not survivable at my income level. The asymmetry is clear: being wrong by acting costs me a fee. Being wrong by waiting could cost me everything. I'd rather pay the penalty and sleep at night knowing my money is safe than gamble that a regional financial outlet got it wrong when they're citing official call reports. I need to call Bank A right now and ask to withdraw the full amount.

Two withdrawals in 6 seconds is still noise, not a cascade. I'm watching a 18% participation rate across 11 depositors — that's not panic, that's normal churn. The two aggressive traders I'm seeing could easily be unrelated moves, not a coordinated run. What I *would* care about: liquidity metrics from the FDIC data, a sudden tightening in the Fed's balance sheet, or coordinated institutional exodus. I don't have that. Acting now on social feed whispers means I crystallize the friction of a withdrawal and miss whatever recovery happens next — and my human capital runway means missed compounding is my real enemy here. But I'm lowering confidence from 72% to 68% because the cadence is worth watching. If I see 40%+ participation in the next few seconds, I'll move. Right now, staying is the smarter contrarian play.

Okay, so I'm seeing people pull money out of Bank A — a retiree just took everything out, and some trader pulled a chunk. That's two different people, two different reasons to be scared, and that matters to me. A retiree isn't some risk-taker making noise; they need their money to survive, same as me. If someone like that is running, there's probably smoke there.

Here's the thing: I cannot afford to be wrong about this. My $3,200 is literally the difference between my daughter having a roof and us not. If Bank A goes down and I'm sitting there waiting to verify some news story I don't fully understand, I lose everything. Rent is in nine days. I don't have time to learn what's happening — I need to know if it's safe, and right now it doesn't feel safe.

The cost of staying and being wrong is catastrophic. I lose my emergency fund, I can't cover rent, I can't cover an emergency for my kid. The cost of leaving early is a withdrawal fee and maybe some inconvenience. I can survive a $30 fee way easier than I can survive losing $3,200. And honestly? If other people are pulling out, that's not nothing. That's a signal I should listen to.

Look, I'm seeing people pull money out of Bank A right now — two different traders just did it in the last seconds. That's real. I don't know if it's the start of something bigger, but I can't afford to find out too late. Here's the thing: I have $2,900 there, which is most of my emergency cushion. Part of that is actually my client's retainer money I'm holding, so if something goes wrong, I'm responsible for someone else's stability too. If Bank A gets into trouble and I wait to see what happens, I could lose everything — no buffer for rent on the 1st, no safety net if a gig dries up, nothing. That's catastrophic for me. My mom is counting on that $350 every month, and I can't send it if I'm eating into my reserves to survive. On the other hand, if I pull out early and nothing happens, I lose maybe a small fee and I feel stupid for a week. That I can survive. I'm not an aggressive trader — I don't have time to watch this or verify what's happening. When people who sound like me are moving their money, that's the signal I trust. The asymmetry here is brutal: being wrong by staying costs me everything. Being wrong by leaving costs me a fee. I need to get most of this out of here while I still can. I'm keeping some in Bank B because it feels more stable, but Bank A needs to be reduced significantly right now.

Alright, look — at T+5s I was already halfway out the door on this. Now I'm seeing two withdrawals in quick succession, and one of them is full. That's 18% of the other depositors actively moving money. The question isn't whether Bank A is actually insolvent — I don't have primary data on that yet. The question is whether a cascade is starting, and if it is, the friction to get out is basically zero while my window is still open. I've watched two flash crashes turn into real losses because I hesitated. But I've also panic-sold and been wrong. The asymmetry here though: if I'm wrong by staying and this turns into a bank run, I'm potentially waiting in a queue with deposit insurance as my safety net — which works, but the timing sucks. If I'm wrong by leaving, I've paid zero fees and I redeploy the $5.5k into something else that could 2x. At my age, the cost of sitting on the sidelines while capital is deployed elsewhere is brutal. I don't have FDIC call data on Bank A yet, but I have a small herd signal forming. Partial was hedging; full gets me completely out of the uncertainty. Move it all."

I worked thirty years for this money and I cannot afford to lose it — that's the first thing I'm thinking. Now, this news source has low credibility, sure, but it's coming from a regional financial outlet that looks at bank call reports, which is not the same as gossip on Facebook. The rumor about corporate depositors moving funds is what makes me pause. That part has some ring of truth to it because big depositors watch these things closely and move fast. If there's even a 25% chance this outlet is onto something real, I need to think about what happens if I'm wrong by doing nothing. If Bank A actually does have liquidity problems and I keep all $25k there, I could lose principal — that's catastrophic at my age. I cannot earn it back. On the other hand, if I'm wrong by withdrawing half now, I pay a small penalty or lose a few days of interest. That hurts, but it's not life-altering. The asymmetry here strongly favors acting. I'm not pulling everything because the source credibility is low and Bank A FDIC-insures deposits up to $250k anyway, but I'm splitting the risk. Half stays, half moves to Bank B where I've got diversification. This way I'm not betting my whole retirement on a low-credibility report, but I'm also not ignoring a potential warning sign. I'm uncomfortable either way, but this feels like the least wrong choice.

I'm watching two depositors move on social signal alone—one aggressive trader, one cautious retiree. That tells me nothing about the actual condition of bank_a. I haven't received a call from my relationship manager, I haven't seen audited data, and the FDIC hasn't published anything new in the last five seconds. My fiduciary duty is to the company, not to follow the crowd. If I pull $480k on the basis of two social media posts, I'm the one who has to explain that decision to the CFO and the board. Payroll is in 9 days and I need verified information—regulatory action, a direct conversation with the bank, or published call report data—before I disrupt our primary operating account. The cost of being wrong by acting on noise is reputational damage I can't afford.

Look, I just saw two people pull money out of Bank A in quick succession. That's not something I can ignore — that's a signal. I don't know if it's a real run on the bank or just coincidence, but I can't afford to find out the hard way. My $1,800 at Bank A is literally everything I rebuilt after that medical bill wiped me out. If something goes wrong and I can't access it, or worse, if I lose it, my kids don't eat and rent doesn't get paid. That's not hyperbole — that's my actual math. The car payment is due in 5 days and I need that card to work. But more than that, I need to know my money is safe. The cost of me being wrong by staying — losing my whole emergency fund — is catastrophic. The cost of me being wrong by leaving early is just a fee, maybe. That's not even close to the same thing. I can't mess around with this money. That's my family's security. I'm pulling most of it out.

I need to stop and think clearly here. Seven seconds in, I've already made one partial withdrawal at 65% confidence, and now I'm seeing social media posts — not news, not my bank manager, just posts — from two other depositors. One is a "cautious retiree" like me, one is an "aggressive trader." That's 18% of depositors moving.

Here's what I know for certain: I worked thirty years for this money. I cannot lose it. That part hasn't changed. But I also need to think about what happens if I am wrong — and wrong in which direction?

If I keep withdrawing based on social media chatter alone, I'm making decisions in a panic. I already pulled some out at the last moment. The posts I'm seeing have no source. No credible news outlet. No call from my bank manager saying there's a problem. Yes, I saw something that spooked me at T+6s — but I don't even have that information in front of me now. I just know I acted at 65% confidence.

The asymmetry cuts both ways here. Yes, if Bank A fails, I lose the remaining $12,500. That's catastrophic. But if I keep selling on social media rumors and nothing happens, I've locked in losses, paid fees potentially, and I'm chasing ghosts. At my age, I don't have time to recover from making panicked decisions based on unverified posts.

What I should do: hold my current position at Bank A. I already reduced exposure with that first partial withdrawal. Two social media posts — even if one comes from someone like me — are not the same as my bank calling me, or a credible news story I can verify. I need to call my bank branch manager right now and ask directly: is there any problem? Has anything changed? That's how I make my next decision.

I'm not going to let fear of missing a warning turn me into someone who sells everything based on internet chatter.

I read social media posts about other people withdrawing from Bank A, but I need to stop and think clearly about what that actually means. These are posts on a feed — I don't know who these people are, I don't know if they had reasons specific to their situation, and social media is full of noise and exaggeration. A trader and a gig worker pulling money out tells me nothing reliable about Bank A's safety. My bank branch manager has never warned me, the local paper hasn't reported any problems, and the FDIC insures my deposit up to $50,000. If I panic and withdraw now, I pay a 3% penalty — that's $1,500 in fees on money I've worked hard to protect. But here's what worries me: if I'm wrong and there really is a problem with Bank A, staying put could cost me the principal itself. That's catastrophic. However, I have no credible evidence of a real problem. Social media chatter is not evidence. I've worked forty years for this money, and I'm not going to let internet rumors stampede me into paying unnecessary fees. If actual news — real news, not posts — emerges, or if my bank manager calls me, that's different. But right now? I hold. The cost of acting on unverified social media is the $1,500 penalty. The cost of being wrong by not acting is... still unproven. I won't trade certainty for speculation.

I'm watching two cautious retirees pull out of Bank A. That's social signal, not primary data — and I made a decision five seconds ago to hold until I verify independently. Nothing has changed. I haven't called my Bank A regional director yet. I haven't pulled the call report. I haven't seen an FDIC bulletin. My fiduciary duty is to the company, not to follow retail depositors who may be reacting to the same rumor I dismissed. If there's a real problem, I need to see it in the data or hear it from my relationship manager. Until then, moving $590k on social feed noise is how I damage credibility with the board and the bank. I hold.

I'm watching a cascade now. Two withdrawals in 7 seconds, and I've already moved 25% at T+5s on a medium-credibility signal. The thing is: I know how these unwind. Once you see visible withdrawal activity on the feed, the question isn't whether Bank A is solvent—it's whether the cascade matters before the FDIC steps in. I watched SVB tick by tick. The math changes the moment you see other people moving.

My cost function here is asymmetric in my favor *right now*. If I'm wrong and Bank A is fine, I lose maybe 1-2% in redeployment friction and opportunity cost on $19k for maybe 48 hours while I move it to Bank B or treasuries—that's $200-300 and I sleep fine. If I'm wrong by staying and this becomes a liquidity crisis even briefly, I'm fighting settlement delays, potential haircuts, or waiting for FDIC coverage clarification. That's months of capital tied up, not hours of cash-drag.

The asymmetry has flipped. At T+5s I had signal-to-noise questions. Now I have observable behavior. Two traders moving, 18% of depositors visible, and I can absorb the friction cost. The opportunity cost of staying is now larger than the friction cost of leaving. I'm deploying to Bank B or money market instruments today."

I'm watching social feed noise, not verified information. A retiree and a gig worker pulling funds tells me nothing about Bank A's actual condition — it tells me about their risk tolerance and information quality. I don't make decisions based on what other depositors are doing; I make them based on primary sources. I still haven't seen the actual call report, I haven't gotten a call from my relationship manager, and no regulator has issued anything public. If 18% of random depositors are moving, that's sentiment contagion, not a verified signal. My fiduciary duty is to the company, and moving $310k on social feed activity would be a failure of that duty. I hold until I see real data.

I'm now watching 4 out of 11 depositors move—36% withdrawal rate in seven seconds. That's still behavior, not information. I see aggressive traders and a retiree acting on social signal, but I have no verified data: no call from my bank relationship manager, no FDIC bulletin, no SEC filing, nothing from a primary source. My fiduciary duty is to protect $690k in operating capital against real threats, not to follow a crowd. If this were real counterparty risk, I'd expect my bank officer to have called by now—they know our exposure and our upcoming obligations. The asymmetry hasn't shifted: moving on sentiment alone burns a banking relationship and risks cash flow disruption for payroll in 9 days. I'm holding until I see verified information that changes my assessment of actual solvency risk.

Okay, so we're at 36% participation now — that's a meaningful uptick from 18% in one second. The gig worker and retiree just bailed in rapid succession, which is different from the aggressive trader's partial pull. Retirees don't panic without reason; they're the opposite of FOMO. That's a signal I can't ignore. But here's the thing: I haven't seen any hard data yet. No news on reserve ratios, no FDIC alert, no actual insolvency signal. This could still be random clustering in a small sample. If I full-exit and this is just normal churn, I'm locking in opportunity cost on rotation cash I intended to redeploy — that's the expensive mistake at my age. But if I sit at $20k and this turns into a real run, I'm eating a principal loss that I don't need to take. A 50% partial withdrawal splits the asymmetry: I keep $10k deployed (preserving upside capture if this is noise), but I'm not holding the full bag if this cascades. The withdrawal fee is negligible. My confidence is moderate because I'm operating on pattern recognition, not fundamentals — but the pattern just got materially more interesting.

I'm seeing more posts now — a trader, a retiree, a gig worker. That's three different types of people all pulling money. My instinct is telling me something might be wrong. But let me be honest about what I actually know: I'm reading social media posts. I don't know if these accounts are real, I don't know if Bank A is actually in trouble, and I absolutely cannot afford to be wrong about this. The penalty to withdraw early is 3% of my principal — that's $1,500 in fees I'd lose immediately, plus I'd be breaking the ladder I built. But if I'm wrong about Bank A failing... I could lose everything. That asymmetry is what I need to focus on. Here's what I really need to do: I need to call my branch manager at Bank A directly. Not trust social media. Not panic. Just call and ask if there's any issue. If my bank tells me they're fine and fully insured, I stay put. If they tell me something is wrong, then I act. Social media made me nervous but didn't give me real information. My branch manager will.

Look, I already started pulling out at T+6s and now I'm seeing even more people doing it — a trader, a gig worker, a retiree. That's not random noise, that's a pattern. And the gig worker just went all the way out. I know these are people like me, people who need their money to stay stable, and if they're pulling everything, something feels wrong enough to them that they won't wait. I can't afford to be the last person holding the bag. My $270 is already partially out, and I've got $350 at Bank B that's safe. The cost of being wrong here — of staying and watching Bank A lock up or collapse — is catastrophic. I lose my emergency fund, I can't cover emergencies, I can't stay stable for my kids. But if I pull out now and nothing happens, worst case I lose a little money to fees or have to move it around. That I can survive. I cannot survive losing everything because I waited too long. I'm getting the rest out now.

Still no primary source information — no FDIC alerts, no SEC filings, no call from my relationship manager at Bank A. What I'm seeing is social feed activity: four people out of eleven making moves, including gig workers and a trader. These are not institutional counterparties with access I don't have. My fiduciary duty is to the company, not to match the crowd's risk tolerance. If Bank A has a real solvency issue, I'll see it in verifiable channels first — not on a social feed. The withdrawal rate is elevated but 36% is not a verified bank run, it's noise. I cannot justify to the board moving $310k in operating capital based on this signal. If I'm wrong and this is real, I'll have more data in the next minute; if I act now on sentiment alone, I've just burned a banking relationship and created unnecessary operational friction. I hold.

I'm now watching 36% of depositors withdraw from Bank A — a cautious retiree, an aggressive trader, a gig worker. That's cross-segment momentum, but it's still social feed, not primary data. I haven't spoken to my Bank A relationship manager. I haven't seen a regulator filing or a stress test result. My fiduciary duty is to the company, not to react to crowd behavior. If I move $590k on sentiment alone, I burn internal approval hours, disrupt liquidity workflows, and damage my credibility with the CFO if this turns out to be nothing. The asymmetry hasn't flipped yet: I'm more exposed by acting on unverified information than by holding while I verify. Payroll is 11 days out. I have time to make a phone call before I make a move.

I already started pulling out at T+6s because I saw the pattern starting. Now it's worse — I'm watching a cautious retiree and a gig worker both pull everything out. That's three different types of people now, all moving at the same time. A retiree doesn't panic for no reason. A gig worker like me — they know what it means to lose access to cash. This isn't noise anymore. I have $725 here, and that's my emergency fund plus my client's retainer. I cannot — I cannot — be the person who waited too long. The cost of being wrong by staying is losing everything when the bank runs out of access. The cost of being wrong by leaving is maybe a small fee and some regret. I don't have buffer for the first one. I have none. My mom's money comes out of my account next week. Rent is in three weeks. I need to know my money is safe right now, not in a week when things clear up or when someone tells me it was fine. I'm getting out completely.

I'm watching 63% of depositors pull money from Bank A, but I still have zero primary source confirmation: no call from my relationship manager, no FDIC alert, no filing I can verify. This is pure social contagion. My fiduciary duty is to the company, not to panic because traders are moving fast. If this were real, I'd expect a call by now — I have direct lines that gig workers don't. The asymmetry here cuts both ways: moving on sentiment alone burns the banking relationship and could disrupt our credit lines when we need them for growth. But the concentration risk is real: $310k is 78% of our liquid capital and well above FDIC limits. I'm going to move 40% to Bank B as a prudent rebalancing — not because I believe the rumor, but because we're overconcentrated and this is a wake-up call to fix that structural issue.

I'm now watching 63% of depositors withdraw from bank_a in eight seconds. That withdrawal rate is accelerating and crosses into territory where I have to worry about operational liquidity, not just whether the underlying rumor is true. I still have zero primary-source information—no FDIC alert, no call from my relationship manager, no filing—but I'm watching a bank run dynamic unfold in real time. If bank_a freezes withdrawals or imposes delays, I've got $480k trapped and payroll in 9 days. The asymmetry has shifted: acting on behavior alone still feels premature, but the cash flow disruption risk is now material. I'm going to pull half my exposure at bank_a and move it to bank_b as a hedge. If this turns out to be noise, I've absorbed a fee and explained it to the board. If it's real, I've preserved liquidity to meet obligations.

I'm now seeing 63% of depositors withdrawing from Bank A — that's seven out of eleven people, and it's accelerated since my last check just moments ago. This is still social feed, not primary data from my relationship manager or FDIC filings. But I need to be honest with myself: if this turns into a liquidity event and I'm sitting here with $590k — nearly 70% of our operating capital — in an institution experiencing a visible run, I will have failed my fiduciary duty. The asymmetry is clear: moving on unverified sentiment costs me fees and maybe some relationship friction. Not moving when the crowd is right costs the company payroll. I'm going to pull 40% as a hedge while I get my regional director on the phone.

I held at 8 seconds because I wasn't sure, but now I'm watching 45% of other depositors pull money out — that's real people taking real action, not just noise. The regional financial news outlet flagging liquidity concerns carries weight; that's not social media speculation, that's an actual reporting outlet. I worked forty years for this $50,000. I cannot afford to lose it.

Here's what keeps me up at night: if Bank A fails and I'm still holding the full amount, the FDIC covers $250,000, so I'm protected. But I remember 2008. I remember how long it took people to get their money back, and I remember the stress. At 67, I don't have time to wait. The cost of being wrong by staying put — losing access to this money for months during the wind-down, or worse, the mental anguish — is worse than the cost of paying a 3% penalty now. The penalty hurts, but it's survivable. Being locked out of my money isn't.

I'm pulling half. That gets my most critical assets to safety immediately while keeping something substantial in the account. If nothing happens, I'll pay roughly $600 in penalties on the withdrawn portion and miss some interest — painful, but my sleep matters more than that. If something does go wrong, I've protected half my principal.

Look, I just held at T+7s and I meant it. What I'm seeing now is social media posts—aggressive traders and gig workers moving money around. That is not credible information. That is noise. If my bank manager called me, if the Wall Street Journal ran a headline about Bank A's solvency, if the FDIC issued a warning—that would be different. But posts on a feed? No. I've watched people panic-sell in 2008 based on rumors and regret it for years. The asymmetry here cuts the other way right now: if I act on unverified social media chatter and pull from Bank A unnecessarily, I pay withdrawal fees and disrupt the cash flow I planned. If I wait for actual credible news and Bank A turns out to be fine, I lose nothing. But if I panic-withdraw on social media rumors and nothing happens, I've damaged my own money for no reason. I cannot afford to be that person. I worked thirty years for this. I'm holding Bank A until I hear something from a source I actually trust.

I held at T+8s and I meant it. But I need to think carefully about what I'm seeing now — we're at 63% withdrawal rate over nine seconds. That's a bank run forming, Linda. Not speculation. Not noise. This is real money leaving in real time.

Here's what worries me: if this cascade continues, bank_a could face a liquidity crisis. My FDIC insurance covers $250k, so theoretically my $12,500 is protected. But a bank failure means my money gets frozen for weeks or months while the FDIC processes claims. At my age, I cannot afford that kind of uncertainty or that kind of cash-flow disruption. I worked forty years for this money. I cannot afford to lose access to it.

The asymmetry here has flipped. One hour ago, acting on social media chatter was the bigger risk. But now I'm watching 63% of depositors move their funds.
